references.text: The people's conviction that John was a prophet is the background for the leaders' fear. They knew that if they rejected John's baptism as merely human, the people would stone them.

All the people, including the tax collectors, acknowledged God's justice when they heard John, and they were baptized with his baptism (Luke 7:29). This shows that the people were convinced that John was a true prophet.
The parallel passage in Matthew 21:26 describes the same event, where the religious leaders feared the crowd because everyone regarded John as a prophet.
The parallel passage in Mark 11:32 similarly states that the leaders feared the people, for all believed that John was truly a prophet.
Herod also feared the crowd because they regarded John as a prophet (Matthew 14:5), which confirms the widespread belief in John's prophetic calling.
Already at John's birth, Zechariah prophesied that the child would be called 'the prophet of the Most High' (Luke 1:76), a conviction the people later held firmly to.
Jesus himself confirmed that John was a prophet, indeed more than a prophet (Matthew 11:9), which supports the people's conviction.
Fear of the people is a recurring theme. Also in Luke 20:19, the scribes and chief priests feared the people when they sought to arrest Jesus.
The fear of being stoned by the people is also mentioned in Acts 5:26, where the temple officers took the apostles away without violence because they were afraid of being stoned by the people.

According to the Mosaic Law, stoning was the penalty for anyone who tried to lead the people away from God (Deuteronomy 13:10), and the leaders feared that the people would treat them as false teachers if they rejected John's prophetic authority.
